> > > Hi again,
> > >
> > > the sample size (N) is used to rescale the sample covariance matrix (S) because sample.cov.rescale=TRUE is the default (see in ?lavOptions). Lavaan uses the "biased" S without Bessel's correction (i.e., the denominator is N) and cov() is the "unbiased" S with Bessels' correction (i.e., the denominator is N-1). Rescaling the sample covariance matrix means multiplying it with *(N-1)/N because it is assumed that you give the "unbiased" S as input.
> > >
> > > library(lavaan)
> > > HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
> > >               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
> > >               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
> > > N <- nrow(HolzingerSwineford1939)
> > >
> > > # unbiased S:

> > > fit_u <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = S_u, sample.nobs = N, sample.cov.rescale=FALSE)
> > > lavInspect(fit_u, "sampstat") # same as S_u
> > >
> > > # biased S:
> > > S_b <- cov(HolzingerSwineford1939[, paste0("x", 1:9)])*(N-1)/N
> > > fit_b <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = S_b, sample.nobs = N, sample.cov.rescale=FALSE)
> > > lavInspect(fit_b, "sampstat") # same as S_b
> > >
> > >
> > > Irrespective of which estimator we use, we have to indicate the correct N to get correct test statistics and model fit statistics (correct as in not "cheating" with N and getting false statistics). I guess we can use robust standard error estimation with giving S as input though.
> > > Further, I guess when "likelihood=wishart" then "sample.cov.rescale=FALSE" and thus the S we give as input is not changed by the N we indicate.
> > >
> > > Hope that helps,
> > >

messages.subject_clean: lavaan syntax duplication
messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Simon. Your question motivated me to think about working with the output of lavParseModelString(). I rarely use this function because it "just" parses the model string, as its name implies. Unlike lavaanify(), it does not create a complete parameter table, which includes parameters such as covariances and error variances that may not need to be specified in the model syntax because they are added automatically by lavaanify() .

Interestingly, in your case, the proper way to achieve what you want, which may also be what I or some others want to do sometimes, is to work on the output of lavParseModelString(), which I arbitrarily call an "incomplete parameter table." Exactly because it just parses the model string and add nothing else, it allows us to generate the original model syntax.

I revised ptable_to_syntax() (https://sfcheung.github.io/semhelpinghands/reference/ptable_to_syntax.html) to work with the output of  lavParseModelString(). However, due to the nature of the output of lavParseModelString(), I disabled this feature by default to prevent accidental usage. To allow  ptable_to_syntax() to work with the output of  lavParseModelString(), set allow_incomplete to TRUE. This feature is for advanced users who know what they are doing.

Please find an illustration at the end of this post. To label unlabelled free parameters, I drafted a simple function, label_free() (similar to Christian's label.param()).  This is the workflow:

- Use  lavParseModelString(),with as.data.frame. = TRUE, to generate an "incomplete parameter table."
- Label the free parameters. You can do it in your own way, or use label_free() .  It depends on the model you are going to work on.
- Use  ptable_to_syntax() to reproduce a model syntax string.

The layout of the reproduced model syntax certainly cannot be identical to the original model syntax. However, it should function in the same way, except for the labels.

Note that, unlike working with a proper parameter table, I do not yet know of a reliable way to compare the output of lavParseModelString(), and so I did not write a version of  compare_ptables() for the output of lavParseModelString(). Therefore, you need to check the output to make sure that the generated syntax is functionally identically to the original model syntax.

The revised function is in the latest version (0.1.9.9) of semhelpinghands at GitHub:

remotes::install_github("sfcheung/semhelpinghands")

Note that there is a lot of possibilities in specifying a model by syntax and I cannot guarantee that these functions will work for all cases (I already know cases in which they will not work and prevent them to work on those cases). Nevertheless, if you only need to do what you want to do in just a few possible models, then it is not difficult to check whether the results produced are what you need.

Personally, I still think it is more reliable to work on the model string itself and use function like gsub(). The process is more transparent and it is also easier check the results. This approach can also keep the layout and comments, which are lost when the string is parsed by lavParseModelString() . However, if the input model syntax must have its free parameters unlabelled, then I do not yet know of a solution that works directly on the model string. If there is one, I would like to know too.

Last, if you discovered any bugs, I would love to know. Thanks.

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

``` r
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-16
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.

library(semhelpinghands)
# Need at least Version 0.1.9.9 of semhelpinghands
# Can be installed from GitHub for now:
# remotes::install_github("sfcheung/semhelpinghands")

input <- "y ~ x1 + x2
          x1 ~~ 1*x1
          x2 ~~ 1*x2
          x1 ~~ x2"

# Create an "incomplete" data frame representation
input_df <- lavParseModelString(input, as.data.frame. = TRUE)

# Define a function to label unlabelled free parameters
label_free <- function(object,
                       pnames = NULL,
                       suffix = "") {
    i <- object$fixed == "" & object$label == ""
    q <- sum(i)
    if (q > 0) {
        if (is.null(pnames)) {
            pnames <- paste0("p", seq_len(q), suffix)
          } else {
            if (length(pnames) != q) {
                stop("The length of panmes ",
                     "does not match ",
                     "the number of unlabelled free parameters")
              }
            pnames <- paste0(pnames, suffix)
          }
        object[i, "label"] <- pnames
        return(object)
      } else {
        stop("No unlabelled free parameters.")
      }
  }

# Examples
# Use auto names for unlabelled parameters

tmp <- label_free(input_df,
                  suffix = "a")
tmp
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           p1a
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           p2a
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                           p3a
output_a <- ptable_to_syntax(tmp,
                             allow_incomplete = TRUE)
cat(output_a, "\n")
#> y ~ p1a*x1 + p2a*x2

#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2

#> x1 ~~ p3a*x2

tmp <- label_free(input_df,
                  suffix = "b")
tmp
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           p1b
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           p2b
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                           p3b
output_b <- ptable_to_syntax(tmp,
                             allow_incomplete = TRUE)
cat(output_b, "\n")
#> y ~ p1b*x1 + p2b*x2

#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2

#> x1 ~~ p3b*x2

# Examples
# Use user-supplied labels

tmp <- label_free(input_df,
                  pnames = c("b1", "b2", "r"),
                  suffix = "a")
tmp
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           b1a
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           b2a
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                            ra
output_a <- ptable_to_syntax(tmp,
                             allow_incomplete = TRUE)
cat(output_a, "\n")
#> y ~ b1a*x1 + b2a*x2

#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2

#> x1 ~~ ra*x2

tmp <- label_free(input_df,
                  pnames = c("b1", "b2", "r"),
                  suffix = "b")
tmp
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           b1b
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           b2b
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                            rb
output_b <- ptable_to_syntax(tmp,
                             allow_incomplete = TRUE)
cat(output_b, "\n")
#> y ~ b1b*x1 + b2b*x2

#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2

#> x1 ~~ rb*x2

# Examples
# Generate a list of model syntax strings

tmps <- mapply(label_free,
               suffix = c("x", "y", "z"),
               MoreArgs = list(object = input_df,
                               pnames = c("b1", "b2", "r")),
               SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
tmps
#> $x
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           b1x
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           b2x
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                            rx
#>
#> $y
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           b1y
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           b2y
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                            ry
#>
#> $z
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           b1z
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           b2z
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                            rz

outputs <- lapply(tmps,
                  ptable_to_syntax,
                  allow_incomplete = TRUE)

cat(outputs[[1]], "\n")
#> y ~ b1x*x1 + b2x*x2

#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2

#> x1 ~~ rx*x2
cat(outputs[[2]], "\n")
#> y ~ b1y*x1 + b2y*x2

#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2

#> x1 ~~ ry*x2
cat(outputs[[3]], "\n")
#> y ~ b1z*x1 + b2z*x2

#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2

#> x1 ~~ rz*x2
```

From: lav...@googlegroups.com <lav...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Shu Fai Cheung (張樹輝) <shufai...@gmail.com>

Subject: Re: lavaan syntax duplication

Thanks, Simon. Your question motivated me to think about working with the output of lavParseModelString(). I rarely use this function because it "just" parses the model string, as its name implies. Unlike lavaanify(), it does not create a complete parameter table, which includes parameters such as covariances and error variances that may not need to be specified in the model syntax because they are added automatically by lavaanify() .

Interestingly, in your case, the proper way to achieve what you want, which may also be what I or some others want to do sometimes, is to work on the output of lavParseModelString(), which I arbitrarily call an "incomplete parameter table." Exactly because it just parses the model string and add nothing else, it allows us to generate the original model syntax.

I revised ptable_to_syntax() (https://sfcheung.github.io/semhelpinghands/reference/ptable_to_syntax.html) to work with the output of  lavParseModelString(). However, due to the nature of the output of lavParseModelString(), I disabled this feature by default to prevent accidental usage. To allow  ptable_to_syntax() to work with the output of  lavParseModelString(), set  allow_incomplete to TRUE. This feature is for advanced users who know what they are doing.

Please find an illustration at the end of this post. To label unlabelled free parameters, I drafted a simple function, label_free() (similar to Christian's label.param()).  This is the workflow:

- Use  lavParseModelString(),with as.data.frame. = TRUE, to generate an "incomplete parameter table."
- Label the free parameters. You can do it in your own way, or use  label_free() .  It depends on the model you are going to work on.
- Use  ptable_to_syntax() to reproduce a model syntax string.

The layout of the reproduced model syntax certainly cannot be identical to the original model syntax. However, it should function in the same way, except for the labels.

Note that, unlike working with a proper parameter table, I do not yet know of a reliable way to compare the output of lavParseModelString(), and so I did not write a version of  compare_ptables() for the output of lavParseModelString(). Therefore, you need to check the output to make sure that the generated syntax is functionally identically to the original model syntax.

The revised function is in the latest version (0.1.9.9) of semhelpinghands at GitHub:

remotes::install_github("sfcheung/semhelpinghands")

Note that there is a lot of possibilities in specifying a model by syntax and I cannot guarantee that these functions will work for all cases (I already know cases in which they will not work and prevent them to work on those cases). Nevertheless, if you only need to do what you want to do in just a few possible models, then it is not difficult to check whether the results produced are what you need.

Personally, I still think it is more reliable to work on the model string itself and use function like gsub(). The process is more transparent and it is also easier check the results. This approach can also keep the layout and comments, which are lost when the string is parsed by lavParseModelString() . However, if the input model syntax must have its free parameters unlabelled, then I do not yet know of a solution that works directly on the model string. If there is one, I would like to know too.

Last, if you discovered any bugs, I would love to know. Thanks.

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

``` r
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-16
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
library(semhelpinghands)
# Need at least Version 0.1.9.9 of semhelpinghands
# Can be installed from GitHub for now:
# remotes::install_github("sfcheung/semhelpinghands")

input <- "y ~ x1 + x2
          x1 ~~ 1*x1
          x2 ~~ 1*x2
          x1 ~~ x2"

# Create an "incomplete" data frame representation
input_df <- lavParseModelString(input, as.data.frame. = TRUE)

# Define a function to label unlabelled free parameters
label_free <- function(object,
                       pnames = NULL,
                       suffix = "") {
    i <- object$fixed == "" & object$label == ""
    q <- sum(i)
    if (q > 0) {
        if (is.null(pnames)) {
            pnames <- paste0("p", seq_len(q), suffix)
          } else {
            if (length(pnames) != q) {
                stop("The length of panmes ",
                     "does not match ",
                     "the number of unlabelled free parameters")
              }
            pnames <- paste0(pnames, suffix)
          }
        object[i, "label"] <- pnames
        return(object)
      } else {
        stop("No unlabelled free parameters.")
      }
  }

# Examples
# Use auto names for unlabelled parameters

tmp <- label_free(input_df,
                  suffix = "a")
tmp
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           p1a
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           p2a
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                           p3a
output_a <- ptable_to_syntax(tmp,
                             allow_incomplete = TRUE)
cat(output_a, "\n")
#> y ~ p1a*x1 + p2a*x2
#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2
#> x1 ~~ p3a*x2

tmp <- label_free(input_df,
                  suffix = "b")
tmp
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           p1b
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           p2b
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                           p3b
output_b <- ptable_to_syntax(tmp,
                             allow_incomplete = TRUE)
cat(output_b, "\n")
#> y ~ p1b*x1 + p2b*x2
#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2
#> x1 ~~ p3b*x2

# Examples
# Use user-supplied labels

tmp <- label_free(input_df,
                  pnames = c("b1", "b2", "r"),
                  suffix = "a")
tmp
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           b1a
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           b2a
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                            ra
output_a <- ptable_to_syntax(tmp,
                             allow_incomplete = TRUE)
cat(output_a, "\n")
#> y ~ b1a*x1 + b2a*x2
#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2
#> x1 ~~ ra*x2

tmp <- label_free(input_df,
                  pnames = c("b1", "b2", "r"),
                  suffix = "b")
tmp
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           b1b
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           b2b
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                            rb
output_b <- ptable_to_syntax(tmp,
                             allow_incomplete = TRUE)
cat(output_b, "\n")
#> y ~ b1b*x1 + b2b*x2
#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2
#> x1 ~~ rb*x2

# Examples
# Generate a list of model syntax strings

tmps <- mapply(label_free,
               suffix = c("x", "y", "z"),
               MoreArgs = list(object = input_df,
                               pnames = c("b1", "b2", "r")),
               SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
tmps
#> $x
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           b1x
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           b2x
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                            rx
#>
#> $y
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           b1y
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           b2y
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                            ry
#>
#> $z
#>   lhs op rhs mod.idx block fixed start lower upper label prior efa rv
#> 1   y  ~  x1       0     1                           b1z
#> 2   y  ~  x2       0     1                           b2z
#> 3  x1 ~~  x1       1     1     1
#> 4  x2 ~~  x2       2     1     1
#> 5  x1 ~~  x2       0     1                            rz

outputs <- lapply(tmps,
                  ptable_to_syntax,
                  allow_incomplete = TRUE)

cat(outputs[[1]], "\n")
#> y ~ b1x*x1 + b2x*x2
#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2
#> x1 ~~ rx*x2
cat(outputs[[2]], "\n")
#> y ~ b1y*x1 + b2y*x2
#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2
#> x1 ~~ ry*x2
cat(outputs[[3]], "\n")
#> y ~ b1z*x1 + b2z*x2
#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2
#> x1 ~~ rz*x2
```

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am performing invariance testing and for some of my factors I get the opposite sign to the cut-offs in literature when comparing the models.

For instance, I have a factor with 7 questions with ordinal data (4 point Likert scale), for which I am comparing three groups, each with ~800 people in.

I have tried the following code:

MI_round.model <- 'A =~ a1 + a2 + a3 + a4 + a5 + a6 + a7'
MI_round <- subset(fulldata,select=c(id,round,a1,a2,a3,a4,a5,a6,a7))

#Config
MI_round_a.config <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = MI_round.model, data = MI_round, ordered=c("a1","a2","a3","a4","a5","a6","a7"), parameterization = "delta", ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016", group = "round")

mod_round_a.config <- as.character(MI_round_a.config)

fit_round_a.config <- cfa(mod_round_a.config, data = MI_round, group="round", ordered=c("a1","a2","a3","a4","a5","a6","a7"), parameterization = "delta")

Summary(fit_round_a.config, fit.measures=TRUE)

#Metric
MI_round_a.metric <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = MI_round.model, data = MI_round, ordered=c("a1","a2","a3","a4","a5","a6","a7"), parameterization = "delta", ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016", group = "round", group.equal="loadings")

mod_round_a.metric <- as.character(MI_round_a.metric)

fit_round_a.metric <- cfa(mod_round_a.metric, data = MI_round, group="round", ordered=c("a1","a2","a3","a4","a5","a6","a7"), parameterization = "delta")

Summary(fit_round_a.metric, fit.measures=TRUE)

#Scalar
MI_round_a.scalar <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = MI_round.model, data = MI_round, ordered=c("a1","a2","a3","a4","a5","a6","a7"), parameterization = "delta", ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016", group = "round", group.equal=c("thresholds","loadings"))

mod_round_a.scalar <- as.character(MI_round_a.scalar)

fit_round_a.scalar <- cfa(mod_round_a.scalar, data = MI_round, group="round", ordered=c("a1","a2","a3","a4","a5","a6","a7"), parameterization = "delta")

Summary(fit_round_a.scalar, fit.measures=TRUE)

These models have good model fit. However, when I compare the models (subtracting config from metric for one comparison and then subtracting metric from scalar for the second and using CompareFit) to test the invariance, I get some results which are the opposite way round from the cut-offs in literature.

Metric - config: ΔCFI = 0,006. ΔRMSEA = -0,020
Scalar - metric: ΔCFI = -0,006. ΔRMSEA = -0,003

As I understand it, the most often used cut-offs for the differences recommended in literature are ΔCFI ≤ -0,01 and ΔRMSEA ≥ 0.015. I am very confused as to why three of my differences are the opposite sign from the cut-offs recommended and I have no idea how to interpret this and where the problem may lie.

I would really appreciate any help and insight on this.

Thank you so much in advance
Zoë

messages.body_plain:
Dear professors

I conduct a multi group CFA, currently with 2 groups (and another group will have to be added later). The scale we use has four factors and two higher order factors, as follows. From the questionnaire, one characteristic is that the questions are once positively (factor 1 and 3)  and once negatively framed (ie. factor 2 and 4). But they build own individual latent factors.

model <- '
factor1 =~ F1 + F2 + F3 + F4 + F5
factor 2 =~ L1 + M2 + M3 + M4 + M5
factor 3 =~ T1 + T2 + T3 + T4 + T5 + T6
factor 4 =~ A1 + A2 + A3 + A4 + A5 + A6

higher1 =~ factor1 + factor2
higher2 =~ factor3 + factor4
'

Problem: My cfa with group = "Group" is not converging properly. However, if I conduct the CFA for each of the groups separately, the model converges.

The first warning message says:
   " the optimizer (NLMINB) claimed the model converged, but not all
    elements of the gradient are (near) zero; the optimizer may not
    have found a local solution use check.gradient = FALSE to skip
    this check."

I added it to my model fitting, which is simply:

fit <- cfa(model,
           data = dtall,
           group = "Group",
           check.gradient = FALSE)
The second error message says:
1: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.
2: In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative

--> What can I do here? The part that keeps me puzzled is that if I have a look at the covariances, the variances are negative of the factor pairs that have positive and negative connotation (so e.g., between factor 1 and factor 2).

Thank you for any input on this case.

Hi, Alissa,

I'm afraid I do not know exactly why exogenous ordinal variables need to be correlated with something, but it is something I've observed in all models I've tested so far. I suppose it has something to do with how polychoric correlations are calculated.

Basically, if you do something like
```{r}
model <- 'DV~sex'
```
with sex treated as an ordinal dichotomous item, lavaan will give an error saying that there are exogenous ordinal items. But if you do

```{r}
model <- 'DV~sex
sex~~age
```
Then, lavaan will analyze the model without complaining.

However, this was just a suggestion of what to try, I'm not sure if this will settle your problem because in your case, the error is lack of variance in the interaction term. I've never done tests with interactions. As a matter of fact, I always thought lavaan couldn't handle interactions, and, in your case, it says the interaction is a logical argument (TRUE/FALSE) with zero observations.
Thus, I believe you'll need to do option 1 or calculate the interaction manually, as explained in Finch, W., & French, B. (2015). Latent variable modeling with R (pp.117-124). Routledge. doi: 10.4324/9781315869797.

P.S.: As I said, I've never tested models with interactions, so I'm not sure this will settle the problem. These are educated guesses based on the error messages you are getting, and I would very much appreciate others opinions.

Best,
Yago

Hello all,

I am using lavaan to test a model that uses different types of variables. There are observed categorical variables that are binary, observed continuous variables, latent continuous variables and a binary dependant variable.

Since I have a dependant variable that is binary, I was trying to use the "ordered" argument in my model fit and I constantly get this error message:
Error in lavaan::lavaan(model = dma.sem.v3.2, data = DMA, ordered = Q13.binaire, : object 'Q13.binaire' not found

Here is my script so far:
library(haven)
library(sjPlot)
library(lavaan)
library(lavaanPlot)
library(semPlot)
options(max.print = 1000000)

DMA <- haven::read_sav(file.choose())

dma.sem.v3.2 <- '
#measurement model
severite.percue =~ Q9 + Q10 + Q11
auto.eff =~ Q46 + Q47 + Q48 + Q49 + Q50 + Q51 + Q52 + Q53

#regressions
Q8 ~ SCORE_CONNAIS + QS1 + QS2.binaire + QS3A.binaire + QS5 + QS7
severite.percue ~ SCORE_CONNAIS + QS1 + QS2.binaire + QS3A.binaire + QS5 + QS7
INDEX_AV_DMA ~ SCORE_CONNAIS + QS1 + QS2.binaire + QS3A.binaire + QS5 + QS7
INDEX_DESAV_DMA ~ SCORE_CONNAIS + QS1 + QS2.binaire + QS3A.binaire + QS5 + QS7
auto.eff ~ SCORE_CONNAIS + QS1 + QS2.binaire + QS3A.binaire + QS5 + QS7
Q13.binaire ~ Q8 + severite.percue + INDEX_AV_DMA + INDEX_DESAV_DMA + auto.eff + Q55 + QS6.binaire + Q54_r1 + Q54_r2 + Q54_r4 + Q54_r5 + Q54_r8 + Q54_r9

#residual correlations
'

fit.dma.sem.v3.2 <- sem(dma.sem.v3.2, data = DMA,
                        ordered = Q13.binaire)
summary(fit.dma.sem.v3.2, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)
fitMeasures(fit.dma.sem.v3.2, c("cfi", "nnfi", "rmsea", "srmr"))
standardizedsolution(fit.dma.sem.v3.2)

How do I solve this error message?

Thank you in advance!

For some arguments in some functions, if you use Q13.binaire, a function will try to find the object named Q13.binaire. It does not exist, and hence the error "object 'Q13.binaire' not found".

If you typed "Q13.binaire", it means a string (a length-one character vector, actually). As far as I know, the argument ordered expects a character vector or TRUE/FALSE.

-- Shu Fai

messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the confusion caused.

With ordered = "Q13.binaire",  lavaan will treat the column named Q13.binaire in the data frame as an ordinal variable, even if it actually contains, say, 0 and 1 (or 1 and 2). If you want to check the content of this column in the data frame, you type this:

DMA$Q13.binaire

I would suggest using head(DMA) to check the content of the data frame first.

By the way, you converted the file to a CSV file. You may want to check whether the conversion of variables with labels, which may be numeric variables representing categorical variables (common in SPSS), is done in the intended way.

Instead of using a CSV file, you can use  haven::read_sav()as you did, and use haven::as_factor() to convert labelled columns to factors, which sem() should support:

https://rdrr.io/cran/haven/man/as_factor.html

This may allow you to remove the error lavaan ERROR: unknown ov.types:haven_labelled .

The conversion for (SPSS) labelled variables to factors is quite complicated (to me) and so you should check the content of the converted dataset before using it in sem().

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

I have some ordinal data from an online survey experiment. There were 3 conditions (treatment 1, treatment 2, control).

I manipulated the social class of targets in this experiment, and gathered data on participant's perception of social class and other variables. I want to see how the perception of social class is related to these others variables, and how this might differ across experimental conditions.

I therefore planned to fit models and check for measurement invariance. This is my first time doing this sort of analysis, and it is far and away the most advanced statistics I've ever done, so I'm struggling to fix the issues myself.

For perceived class, I collected perceptions on: education level, job prestige, income, and a judgement of social class itself.  I expected a simple 1 factor solution.

This one factor solution (Perceived class =~ education + job prestige + income + social class) fits the dataset as a whole and treatment 1 well. However, it fits treatment 2 and control poorly.

I have mainly tried to tackle treatment 2 so far, and feel like I am in a real rut with it.

For treatment 2, the factor loadings are much higher than they are for treatment 1, but the fit is worse. The data is distributed differently to treatment 1, but I believe this reflects differences caused by the treatment. I have tried amending the model based on modification indices but this gives me impossible TLI indicies (1.016) and virtually impossible RMSEA indicies (0.000). I've tried removing the lowest loading item, but then the model is just identified so I can't actually get any fit measures.

As I want to compare the differences between groups, I need to establish configural invariance, but can't because the model fits poorly and I can't find a way to change it.

The best lead I have found to fix the issue was around freeing the item thresholds between groups, but I have no idea if that is appropriate or not.

Any help or suggestions massively appreciated

This is a pretty complex model for a beginner. Did you run a mediation model and a moderation model and interpret those?

We don't know what the defined parameters are because we can't see your code, and presumably 'I' is the interaction effect?  How was it created? That's not a great name for a variable, by the way.

P-values of intercepts are generally not interesting - they are arbitrary and you don't care if they are significant.  (You can add a constant to your variables, and nothing that matters will change, except the intercepts/)

Variances are also uninteresting. A variance must be above zero - it's the sum of squares (or it could be zero, under unusual circumstances) unless something has gone wrong,  so the fact that it is statistically significant means it's not zero, which you were pretty sure about before you ran the model.

It appears that you have one statistically significant effect that might be interesting, which is M2 -> Y. If your defined parameters are the indirect effects, then they are not significant, so it doesn't look like you have evidence of an indirect effect.

There are whole books on mediation (and whole books on  moderation, and whole books on mediation and moderation) so it's a little bit difficult to give general advice and citations. Do you have more specific questions?

Remember, the aim of  a statistical model is to try to uncover the truth. The aim is not to obtain a statistically significant result; not getting a significant result is not a failure, and doesn't mean that there's something wrong.

Jeremy

Hi Andi,

I don't have a solution, but I have a couple of suggestions.

 - Paste your code into the email - that way if someone wants to try it to run it, they can.

 - Include all your code - you (presumably) have some library calls at the top, but I don't know what they are. You have a function called model.path(), but I don't know where this comes from (and sometimes this can be worse, I can assume I know the package it comes from, but it actually comes from a different package.

- I'm not familiar with the paper Donnelly et al. 2021. If you post the full reference, I can find it. Even better, save me the effort and give me a link to click on. Even more better, if you can, make sure that the link is not behind a paywall. You might have access, but I might not.

- Bonus suggestion: you can avoid the problem above by qualifying your function names - that is specifying the package the function comes from, by writing: package::function(). That makes it easier to read and can also avoid some problems. Example:
Let's say you're running your model, so you load the lavaan package and run your model:

  library(lavaan)
  sem(my_model, my_data)

You want to explore a bit, so you load the sem package:

   library(sem)

Now you run:

  sem(my_model, my_data)

And you get all sorts of weird errors (or perhaps worse, you don't get all sorts of weird errors).  The first time you ran the sem command, it used lavaan::sem(), the second time it used sem::sem(), so the running the same code in the same file did a different thing - this can be very irritating to debug (and it might be that you didn't even load the sem package, but you loaded another package that had sem as a dependency.  You might have even done this in a separate R script that you were doing something different in. (So you restart R and the error disappears.)

Avoid this by running:

sem::sem(my_model, my_data)

Or

lavaan::sem(my_model, my_data)

Apologies that that email got quite long, and also didn't answer your question. If I didn't have some work to do, I wouldn't have spent the time on this. :)

Good luck!

jeremy

thank you for the suggestions! the simsem package is used, and i adapted the code from here: https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13428-022-01996-0
the model syntax: userParams <- "..." is specified with lavaan package syntax

N.per.group <- 50 # balanced group sample sizes
designMatrix <- expand.grid(X = 1, W = 1:0)
designMatrix$XW <- designMatrix$X * designMatrix$W # interaction
exoData <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:N.per.group, function(i)
  designMatrix))
exoData$X <- sample(1:5, size = 100, replace = TRUE)

a.w0 <- .5 # effect of X on M when moderator (W) == 0
a.mod <- .3 # how much “a” path is moderated by W (i.e., interaction)
b.w0 <- .4 # effect of M on Y when moderator (W) == 0
b.mod <- 0 # no moderating effect on “b” path
c.w0 <-.2 # effect of X on Y when moderator (W) == 0
c.mod <- 0 # no moderating effect on “c” path
w.M <- .2 # simple effect of moderator (W) on M when X == 0
w.Y <- -.1 # simple effect of moderator (W) on Y when X == 0
kappa.free <- kappa.pop <- matrix(NA, # estimate all effects
                                     nrow = 2, # 2 outcomes (M and Y)
                                     ncol = 3, # dummy coded X, W, XW
                                     dimnames = list(c("M", "Y"),names(exoData)))
kappa.free["M","X"] <- "a.w0" # label free parameters
kappa.free["M","W"] <- "w.M" # (to define indirect effects)
kappa.free["M","XW"] <- "a.mod"
kappa.free["Y","X"] <- "c.w0"
kappa.free["Y","W"] <- "w.Y"
kappa.free["Y","XW"] <- 0 # fixed to 0; label “c.mod” to free
kappa.pop["M","X"] <- a.w0 # set population parameters
kappa.pop["M","W"] <- w.M # (defined above)
kappa.pop["M","XW"] <- a.mod
kappa.pop["Y","X"] <- c.w0
kappa.pop["Y","W"] <- w.Y
kappa.pop["Y","XW"] <- c.mod
exoPaths <- bind(free = kappa.free, popParam = kappa.pop)
beta.free <- beta.pop <- matrix(0, nrow = 2, ncol = 2,
                                   dimnames = list(c("M","Y"), c("M","Y")))
beta.free["Y","M"] <- "b"
beta.pop["Y","M"] <- b.w0
endoPaths <- bind(free = beta.free, popParam = beta.pop)
(exoCov <- cov.wt(exoData, method = "ML"))$cov
residVar <- findFactorResidualVar(beta = beta.pop, corPsi = diag(2),
                                  gamma = kappa.pop, covcov = exoCov$cov)
(heteroVar <- list(binds(free = diag(as.numeric(NA), 2),
                         popParam = residVar)))
userParams <- '
ind.w0 := a.w0 * b
ind.w1 := (a.w0 + a.mod) * b
ind.diff := a.mod * b

'

modMed1 <- simsem::model.path(BE = endoPaths, RPS = residCor,
                         KA = exoPaths, con = userParams,
                         indLab = rownames(kappa.free),
                         covLab = colnames(kappa.free))
sim1 <- sim(nRep = 10, model = modMed1, covData = exoData,
               n = nrow(exoData), seed = 2023, outfun = rejectMCCI,
               meanstructure = FALSE)
rejectMCCI <- function(object){
  CIs <- semTools::monteCarloCI(object)
  apply(CIs, margin = 1, function(CI) 0 < CI["ci.lower"] | 0 > CI["ci.upper"])
}

summaryParam(sim1, matchParam = TRUE, digits = 3)
testMCCI <- do.call(rbind, simsem::getExtraOutput(sim1))
colMeans(testMCCI) # empirical estimate of power for Monte Carlo CIs

eta_cmr =~ 1*cmr1 + 1*cmr2 + 1*cmr3 + 1*cmr4 + 1*cmr5 + 1*cmr6

messages.subject_clean: WLSMV and ordered categorical variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I myself rarely use the value "WLSMV" directly to handle ordered categorical variable. I will just use the argument  "ordered" and lets lavaan to set other options, including the estimator.

In lavaan, setting estimator to "WLSMV" actually sets the estimator to "DWLS" (the same method used in Mplus), and sets some other options:

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/Nymu7jmVUk8/m/Su_dhLMgBwAJ

As far as I know, in Mplus, WLSMV is used along with the option CATEGORICAL (at least in the examples I found in the manual). I did a quick test and confirmed that, if I fit a model with WLSMV and did not specify and variable as ordered categorical, a warning will be raised:

*** WARNING in ANALYSIS command
  Estimator WLSMV is not available for analysis with all continuous variables.
  Default estimator will be used.
   1 WARNING(S) FOUND IN THE INPUT INSTRUCTIONS

This confirmed that, in Mplus, WLSMV is supposed to be used when some variables are declared ordered categorical, and is not supposed to be used when all variables are treated as continuous.

However, this is not the case for lavaan. I can set estimator to "WLSMV" even if the model has no categorical variables:

``` r
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-17.1897
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, estimator = "WLSMV")
fit
#> lavaan 0.6.17.1897 ended normally after 44 iterations
#>
#>   Estimator                                       DWLS
#>   Optimization method                           NLMINB
#>   Number of model parameters                        21
#>
#>   Number of observations                           301
#>
#> Model Test User Model:
#>                                               Standard      Scaled
#>   Test Statistic                                43.902      79.342
#>   Degrees of freedom                                24          24
#>   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.008       0.000
#>   Scaling correction factor                                  0.598
#>   Shift parameter                                            5.867
#>     simple second-order correction
lavInspect(fit, "ordered")
#> character(0)
```

<sup>Created on 2023-10-27 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I asked this question because I noticed that some users set estimator to "WLSMV" to handle ordered categorical variables. They are doing the right thing, but only for the estimator. They did not use "ordered" to specify which variables are ordered categorical, and lavaan faithfully does what it is told to do, using DWLS (as in Mplus). They may not know that ordered categorical variables are not treated as such in lavaan, without using "ordered"

Is this an intended behavior of lavaan?

Users of Mplus may not notice this difference, and believe incorrectly that setting the estimator to "WLSMV" is enough to handle ordered categorical variables.

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject_clean: CFA with FIML and factor score
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm using lavaan cfa() and lavPredict() to calculate factor scores. I'm curious about how using FIML when fitting a CFA model affects the factor scores generated by lavPredict() based on the CFA result.

Here's the script that I used:

cfa.cog <- 'LTM =~ m1 + m2 + m3 + m4'
fit.cog <- cfa(cfa.cog, data = df.ndi, meanstructure=TRUE, missing="fiml")
fscores <- lavPredict(fit.cog, method = "regression")

In my dataset, 5 out of 99 subjects have missing values in at least one of the scores. I expected to obtain factor scores for the 94 subjects without missing values as a result of running lavPredict() with the method set to "regression because you need raw scores to calculate a factor score using the regression method, and adding missing="fiml" doesn't impute missing values. However, I found out that lavPredic() generated factor scores for all of the 99 subjects.

Could someone please explain how using FIML when fitting a CFA model affects lavPredict() to calculate factor scores for subjects with missing values?

Thank you so much for your help!

-Youjin

messages.body_plain:
Kim, you will want to check out the formulas for these indices, in any standard text. RMSEA and CFI use the quantity max(chi-square - DF, 0). So if your chi-square is less than degrees of freedom, the quantity is 0. This explains why your RMSEA is 0 and CFI is 1.
TLI is not (like CFI is) normed so that it must fall between 0 and 1. Its numerator uses the ratio chi-square / DF and its denominator uses the quantity 1. So pretty much whenever chi-square is less than DF, numerator will exceed denominator, giving TLI > 1.
